title: Simple Addition Worksheets for Class 1: The First Sums (Within 5, Then 10) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Simple Addition Worksheets for Class 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: The very first simple addition worksheets for Class 1 — sums within 5 then within 10, counting on with objects, bonds to ten, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Before a child can make ten or add in their head, they need the gentlest possible start: sums within 5, then within 10, with pictures they can count. Here is what a good beginner worksheet looks like and how to use it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The first addition worksheet a Class 1 child ever meets should not have 8 + 5 on it. If it does, put it away. A six-year-old who is still learning what the plus sign even means needs sums like 2 + 1 and 3 + 2 — small numbers, with a picture of two apples and one apple sitting right next to the question so they can point and count. That is what a genuinely simple addition worksheet for Class 1 looks like, and getting this beginning right matters more than most parents expect.

I have watched plenty of bright children decide they are ‘bad at maths’ in the first month of Class 1, purely because the worksheet in front of them jumped ahead of where they were. The fix is almost always to go back, slow down, and rebuild from sums within 5. So before you print anything, here is the order that actually works and what each stage should contain.

What a simple addition worksheet for Class 1 should contain

A beginner sheet has three jobs: keep the numbers tiny, keep something countable on the page, and repeat the same idea enough times that it stops feeling new. The best ones I use for early Class 1 have these features:

  • Sums within 5 first — 1 + 1 up to 4 + 1, nothing that crosses five.
  • Pictures beside the numbers — dots, stars or objects the child physically counts, not just bare digits.
  • One idea per sheet — a whole page of ‘add 1’ before a whole page of ‘add 2’.
  • Plenty of white space — five or six large questions, not thirty cramped ones.
  • An answer key for the adult — so you can check without redoing the maths yourself.

Stage 1: addition within 5 with objects

Start here even if your child seems ready for more. Put out three buttons, then two more, and ask ‘how many altogether?’ Let them touch each one as they count. The worksheet mirrors this: a question like 3 + 2 with three dots and two dots printed next to it. The child counts the dots, writes 5, and slowly learns that the plus sign means ‘put together and count’.

Do not rush to remove the objects. Fingers, beans, coins — anything concrete is a friend at this stage, not a crutch to be embarrassed about. The abstraction comes later, on its own.

Stage 2: counting on instead of counting all

The first real strategy is counting on. Most beginners count everything twice — for 4 + 2 they count out four, then two, then start again at one and count all six. Counting on means holding the four in your head and going ‘four… five, six’. It is the first time a child adds without starting over.

A neat trick to teach alongside it: start from the bigger number. Counting on to solve 2 + 5 is five hops from two, but only two hops from five. Children genuinely light up when they notice 2 + 5 and 5 + 2 both land on seven. That discovery — that order does not change the answer — is a Class 1 milestone worth pausing on.

Stage 3: addition within 10 and bonds to ten

Once sums within 5 are comfortable, stretch to within 10: 6 + 3, 5 + 4, 7 + 2. This is also the moment to introduce the number bonds to ten — the pairs that make exactly ten (1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5). A child who knows these cold finds every later step of arithmetic easier for years. A ten-frame worksheet, two rows of five boxes, is the single best tool here; if you want a deeper walkthrough of this stage, our guide on addition within 10 for Grade 1 covers it in full.

How to use these worksheets at home

Ten minutes a day beats an hour on a Sunday. Sit beside your child, not across from them, and let them explain their counting out loud — you learn far more from how they got 6 + 3 than from whether the answer is right. If they miss one, do not correct it instantly. Hand them the buttons and let them find it themselves.

One honest caveat: resist the urge to time them. Speed at this age is a trap. A child who works out 7 + 2 slowly but understands why is in a far stronger position than one who blurts answers they cannot explain. In my experience teaching six-year-olds, fluency arrives on its own once the thinking underneath is solid — and never arrives at all if you skip these first stages to chase it.

When your child can add within 10 without pictures, they are ready for the next chapter: making ten to cross into the teens, and the five core strategies in our post on how to teach addition to Grade 1.

quiz.title: Simple Addition Quiz for Class 1
quiz.intro: Eight easy questions on sums within 10 — counting on and a bond to ten. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Count two, then two more: 1, 2, 3, 4. So 2 + 2 = 4.
Start from the bigger number 3 and count on two: 4, 5. So 3 + 2 = 5.
Count on from 5 four times: 6, 7, 8, 9. So 5 + 4 = 9.
Adding one gives the very next number. After 6 comes 7.
6 and 4 fill a ten-frame exactly. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.
Count on from 5 three times: 6, 7, 8. So 5 + 3 = 8.
7 and 3 are a bond to ten, so 7 + 3 = 10.

faq.q: What should the first Class 1 addition worksheets cover?
faq.a: Sums within 5 with pictures the child can count — things like 2 + 1 and 3 + 2 — before moving to within 10. Keep it to five or six large questions per page with plenty of space, and one idea at a time.

faq.q: Is it fine for my child to count on fingers?
faq.a: Yes, at the start. Fingers, buttons and dots make the maths concrete and are a genuine help, not a bad habit. The aim is to give better tools like counting on and bonds to ten so the child chooses to leave fingers behind naturally.

faq.q: When is a child ready for sums past 10?
faq.a: Once they can add within 10 without needing pictures, and they know most of the number bonds to ten. Then you introduce making ten to cross into the teens — that is the next stage, not a beginner one.

faq.q: How much daily practice does a beginner need?
faq.a: About ten focused minutes a day, sitting beside your child while they count out loud, beats a long weekly session. At this age consistency matters far more than length, and avoid timing them.
